newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World trade body urged to eye dairy, sugar accords.
newsitem.headline: World trade body urged to eye dairy, sugar accords.

text.p: A global think-tank on Wednesday urged member countries of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to move towards formal agreements bringing the highly-protected dairy and sugar industries under free trade trading rules.

At the same time, European chemical industry chiefs called for the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore in December to keep up the pace of trade liberalisation by adopting clear initiatives like standardisation of customs procedures.

The calls were issued at separate news conferences as the 21-month-old trade body entered the final lap of a debate on what should be on the agenda for the December gathering, which could lead to the launch of a new global trade round.

Presenting separate papers on the world dairy and sugar trade, the Washington-based International Policy Council on Agriculture, Food and Trade (IPC) said reform in both areas was vital before it was forced on the two sectors.
It said in a statement the Singapore meeting should agree on starting discussions on "a timetable and basis for multilateral reform of global sugar and dairy policies."

"The sugar market is riddled with distortions because of protection, including export subsidies and quotas, and a more rational and liberalised system would bring huge benefit to the world economy," said IPC sugar specialist Sir Michael Franklin.

Franklin, a former top civil servant at Britain's Ministry of Agriculture, said barriers to imports in the European Union, the United States and Japan kept out sugar from efficient producers in many developing countries.

Aart de Zeuw, a former senior Netherlands trade diplomat, said the subsidies and quotas used by major powers to protect their own dairy industries and those of favoured suppliers were also doomed to disappear.
"The next round of world trade negotiations will continue to open up this market also, and it would be wise for governments and the sector to start preparing themselves now," he told reporters.
The two said reform in the two areas would eventually bring down prices for the consumer, although in some trading powers where protection was high -- especially the EU -- they would initially rise.

"Let the market decide prices in the long term. Where social and environmental problems make it essential to soften the impact on farmers and farming communities, direct income support unlinked to production should replace subsidies," said de Zeuw.

During the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of trade negotiations under the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the United States and the EU reached an accord attacking grain subsidies under pressure from other producer-powers.

But the dairy sector, managed under the 1980 International Dairy Agreement, was scarcely touched -- largely because of resistance from the EU, Canada, Japan and Switzerland which are reluctant to tackle the subsidy system.
In its own initiative aimed at Singapore, the European Chemical Industry Council (CEFIC) said it wanted the WTO ministers' gathering to endorse further liberalisation.

David Wakeford of Britain's ICI, chairman of CEFIC's External Trade Committee, said the European industry would support the total elimination of chemical tariffs by the year 2010 if all the WTO's 123 members agreed.

"The Ministerial Meeting should also maintain the momentum of liberalisation by adopting a few focussed initiatives," he said. "Simplification and standardisation of customs procedures would address one of the biggest non-tariff barriers to international trade."
